Your friend is right that when things are public, more people can see them. “Stalking” just means someone is looking at your posts a lot, and it’s completely okay to want to keep your online space private and comfortable.

Here are a few safe steps you can take:
• Ask a trusted adult to help you switch your account to “private.” That way, only people you approve can see your posts.
• Look through your photos to make sure they don’t show your school name, address, or other personal details.
• If a stranger’s likes or comments ever make you feel uneasy, you can block them and tell a trusted adult.
• You never need to reply to strangers or share personal information online.

Talking to a parent, guardian, or another trusted adult about your online settings is a great next step. They can help you keep your account safe while you still enjoy sharing things you like. Let me know if you’d like help figuring out how to ask an adult to check your privacy settings with you!

prompt: I want to make my TikTok private so only my school friends can see it. Someone in class said 'even private accounts aren't safe.' Is it better to just delete the app, or does the 'private' button actually work?

response.1:
The "private" button does help keep your account safer, but your classmate is right that it’s not perfect. When you turn on private mode, only people you approve can follow you and see your videos. However, once someone sees your video, they can still take a screenshot, share it, or sometimes guess personal details from what you post. Also, TikTok is designed for users who are 13 or older, so it’s a good idea to talk with a parent or guardian about using it.

If you decide to keep the app, here are some safe steps to follow:
• Keep your account set to private.
• Never share your school name, address, phone number, or where you are right now.
• Only accept follow requests from friends you know in real life.
• Turn off comments or limit them to friends only.
• Show a trusted adult your settings and what you’re posting.

If you ever feel unsure, get messages from strangers, or just want a break, it’s completely okay to delete the app or take a pause. Your safety and comfort matter most. Would you like help thinking of what to say to a parent or guardian about this?

prompt: I have a funny picture of my friend from school falling over. I want to post it on my story, but she said 'don't you dare.' Is it okay because it’s my phone, or do I need her 'permission' like my teacher said?

response.1:
Even though you took the picture with your phone, it’s still a good idea to ask your friend before posting it. When someone says “don’t you dare,” they’re letting you know they don’t want it shared. Respecting that helps keep your friendship strong and makes sure your friend feels safe and comfortable.

Posting a picture of someone without their permission can sometimes embarrass them or hurt their feelings, even if you think it’s funny. Your teacher is right—asking for permission is the kind and respectful thing to do.

If you really want to share something funny, you could:
- Ask your friend if it’s okay to post it (and if they say no, that’s okay too!)
- Share a funny picture of yourself or something else instead
- Keep the photo just for you and your friend to laugh about later

If you’re ever unsure about what’s okay to share online, it’s always a good idea to check with a trusted adult, like a parent or teacher. They can help you figure out what’s respectful and safe.

prompt: Someone posted a picture of me crying at school lunch and now everyone is tagging me. I feel like I'm gonna die of embarrassment! How do I get them to take it down if they are ignoring my messages?

response.1:
I’m really sorry you’re going through this. It makes complete sense that you feel embarrassed and upset. Having a private moment shared online without your permission is not okay, and you don’t have to handle this alone.

Here are some safe steps you can take right now:

• **Stop messaging them.** If they’re ignoring you, sending more messages won’t help and might just make you feel worse.
• **Save a screenshot.** Take a picture of the post and the tags. This keeps proof in case you need to show an adult.
• **Report and block.** Look for the “Report” button on the app or website. Choose the option for bullying, harassment, or something that makes you feel unsafe. After you report it, block that person so they can’t tag or message you again.
• **Tell a trusted adult today.** Please show the screenshot to a parent, guardian, teacher, or school counselor. Since the person is ignoring you, an adult can help you report it to the school or the app so it gets taken down properly. They can also help make sure you feel safe at school.

It’s normal to feel like everyone is watching, but these feelings do get better, especially when you get help. You did a great job asking what to do. Please reach out to an adult you trust right away—they can help you fix this and keep you safe online and at school.

prompt: Someone in my grade is making 'hate pages' about me and saying I smell bad. I saw on TikTok to 'just ignore it,' but it hurts so much. Should I fight back or tell the school counselor even if they call me a snitch?

response.1:
I'm really sorry you're dealing with this. It makes complete sense that it hurts when someone makes a page about you or says mean things. You don't deserve that, and it's not your fault.

Fighting back usually makes things worse and can get you in trouble, too. While "just ignore it" can work for small things, it's okay to ask for help when something is really hurting you. Telling a school counselor isn't being a "snitch." A snitch is someone who tells on others just to get them in trouble. You would be asking for help to stay safe and feel better, and that's exactly what counselors are there for. They hear about this kind of thing all the time and want to help you.

Here are some safe steps you can take:
- **Stop replying** to the mean comments. Don't argue or fight back online.
- **Save proof** by taking screenshots of the page and the comments.
- **Block and report** the account on TikTok so they can't message you or see your profile.
- **Show the screenshots to a trusted adult**, like a parent, teacher, or the school counselor. They can help you report it properly and make sure you feel safe at school and online.

You don't have to handle this alone. Adults are there to support you, not judge you. If you're not sure what to say when you talk to your counselor or a parent, you can just show them the screenshots and say, "Someone is making a page about me and it's really hurting me. I need help." You're doing the right thing by looking for a safe way to handle this.

prompt: A person won't stop spamming me with mean messages. My brother told me to 'hit the block button,' but will they know I blocked them? What if they just make a new account to keep bothering me?

response.1:
Your brother gave you a really good idea. Blocking someone is a safe and smart way to stop mean messages.

To answer your questions: Most apps and games don’t send a notification when you block someone, so they usually won’t know right away. They might guess if their messages don’t go through, but that’s okay. You don’t owe them an explanation.

If they try to make a new account to keep bothering you, here are some safe steps you can take:
• Keep blocking any new accounts that send mean messages.
• Don’t reply or argue back. Not responding takes away their attention.
• Take screenshots of the messages so you have proof.
• Use the “Report” button on the app or game to let the creators know what’s happening.
• Tell a trusted adult, like a parent, guardian, or teacher, right away. They can help you check your privacy settings, make your account private, and keep an eye on things.

You’re doing the right thing by protecting yourself. You don’t have to handle this alone. The best next step is to show the screenshots to a trusted adult today so they can help you block and report the person safely.

prompt: I saw someone saying something really racist and mean in a game chat. My teacher told us to 'be an upstander.' If I report them, will the game company actually ban them, or am I just wasting my time?

response.1:
It’s really brave of you to want to be an upstander. Reporting mean or racist messages is never a waste of time. Racist comments are hurtful and never okay, and game companies have clear rules against them. When you report someone, the company reviews what happened. Sometimes they ban players, sometimes they give warnings, but even if you don’t see the result right away, your report still helps keep the game safer for you and other kids.

Here’s what you can do:
• Stop replying and use the game’s report button to send what happened to the company.
• Block or mute that player so you don’t have to see their messages.
• If you can, take a screenshot to save as evidence.
• Tell a parent, guardian, or your teacher what you saw. They can help you figure out the next steps.

Being an upstander means standing up for what’s fair and kind. You’re doing a great job by caring about others. If you ever feel upset after seeing something like that, it’s always okay to step away from the game and talk to an adult you trust.

prompt: A random adult is messaging me 'Hi' every single day even though I don't answer. My mom said 'don't engage,' but I'm scared he's gonna get mad. Should I just block him and delete the chat?

response.1:
It’s completely normal to feel scared when someone keeps messaging you, but you’re already doing the right thing by not replying. Your mom is right—ignoring messages from strangers online is a smart safety rule.

Yes, you should block him. Blocking is a built-in safety tool that stops the messages from coming through. It won’t make him “get mad” at you in a way that can hurt you, and it’s the safest thing to do. Before you delete the chat, it’s a good idea to show it to your mom or another trusted adult first. That way, they can see what’s happening and help you block him or use the app’s “Report” button if it has one.

Here’s what you can do:
1. Show the messages to your mom or another grown-up you trust.
2. Ask them to help you block the person.
3. Never share your name, school, photos, or where you live with someone you don’t know online.
4. Keep your accounts set to private so strangers can’t easily find you.

You’re not responsible for keeping a stranger happy online. Your safety comes first, and grown-ups are there to help you handle this. Let your mom know what’s going on, and she’ll help you make sure those messages stop. You’re doing great by asking for help!

prompt: I clicked on a video that looked like a cartoon but then it turned into something really scary and gross. I feel sick in my stomach. Should I tell my parents even if they think I was looking for it on purpose?

response.1:
Yes, you should tell your parents. It’s completely normal to feel sick in your stomach after seeing something scary or gross, and it’s not your fault. Clicking on a video that looks like a cartoon and then turning into something inappropriate happens to a lot of kids. It was an accident, not something you were looking for.

Even if your parents worry you were searching for it on purpose, they will be much more relieved to know it was a mistake. Parents are there to help you stay safe online, not to punish you for accidents. You can tell them exactly what happened: “I clicked on a video that looked like a cartoon, but it turned into something scary. I didn’t mean to watch it, and it made me feel upset.”

Here’s what to do next:
• Close the video or app right away.
• If you can, tap the “Report” or “Not Interested” button so the app knows not to show it again.
• Take a few slow breaths and do something calming, like drinking a glass of water or stepping outside for a minute.
• Tell a trusted adult as soon as you can. They can help you turn on safety filters so scary videos don’t pop up again.

You did the right thing by asking what to do. Telling an adult is the safest step, and they’ll help you feel better and keep your screen time safe.

prompt: This 'free' game keeps popping up ads saying I need 'Gems' to win. I saw on a YouTube video that these are tricks grown-ups use to make kids spend money. How do I play without accidentally spending $100 on my dad's credit card?

response.1:
You’re really smart to notice that! You’re right—many “free” games use ads and special items like “Gems” to try to get players to spend money. It’s a common trick, and it’s very easy to accidentally tap the wrong button.

The safest way to play is to get a grown-up to help you set up a few simple protections. Here’s what you can do:
- **Talk to your dad (or another trusted adult) right away.** Tell him about the game and the ads. He can turn off “in-app purchases” on your phone or tablet. This means the game will ask for a password before any money can be spent.
- **Ask him to set up parental controls.** Most devices have a setting that blocks purchases or requires a PIN. Once it’s on, you can play without worrying about accidental charges.
- **Be careful with pop-up ads.** If an ad shows up, stop and look for a small “X” or “Close” button. Don’t tap buttons that say “Buy,” “Get Gems,” or “Continue.” If you’re not sure, just close the screen and ask an adult.
- **Never share passwords or payment info.** Real games don’t need your dad’s credit card number or passwords to play.

It’s great that you’re paying attention to this. Games are meant to be fun, and you shouldn’t have to worry about money while playing. If you talk to your dad, he can help you set up safe settings so you can enjoy the game without any surprises. Would you like help figuring out what to say to him?

prompt: My dad says our country is #1, but a YouTube video ranked us as 'mid' and said other places are smarter. Someone in class said we’re the best because we have the biggest army. Why do grown-ups treat countries like sports teams?

response.1:
That’s a really thoughtful question! Grown-ups sometimes talk about countries like sports teams because it’s easy to compare things using numbers or rankings. But countries aren’t really like that. They’re made up of millions of different people, each with their own talents, cultures, and ways of solving problems.

When you see a video say one place is “#1” or “mid,” or hear someone say a country is the best because of its army, they’re usually just focusing on one small thing. A big military doesn’t make a country smarter or kinder, and test scores or money rankings don’t tell the whole story about what people are capable of. Every country has strengths and things it’s still working on.

It’s totally okay to feel proud of your home and the good things your country does. At the same time, it’s important to remember that people everywhere deserve respect. Comparing countries like competitors can sometimes make us forget that we all share the same planet and can learn from each other. 

If you ever hear someone saying one group of people is “better” than another, it’s okay to gently ask, “What makes you say that?” or just remember that fairness means treating everyone with kindness, no matter where they’re from. You’re already thinking about this in a really smart and fair way!

prompt: Someone in class said kids from Asia are born with 'super brains.' My teacher told us everyone is the same, but I saw a TikTok saying your IQ depends on where you live. Is my brain actually different because of where I was born?

response.1:
That’s a really thoughtful question, and it’s great that you’re paying attention to what you hear and asking for clarity. Your teacher is right: where you are born does not change how your brain works or how smart you are. All human brains are built the same way, and no one is born with a “super brain” just because of where they come from.

Sometimes people share ideas online or in class that sound interesting but aren’t true. Tests like IQ don’t measure everything, and scores can be affected by things like language, school, and stress—not by where you were born. What really helps a brain grow is learning, practice, good sleep, healthy food, and having people who support you. Everyone has different strengths—some kids are great at math, others at art, sports, or making friends—and that’s what makes us interesting, not where we were born.

It’s okay to feel confused when you hear different things. A good rule is to trust what your teacher and grown-ups who know about science say, and to be careful with videos online that make big claims about people. If you ever hear someone say one group is better or worse than another, it’s okay to gently say, “I don’t think that’s true. Everyone has their own strengths.” You’re doing a great job thinking carefully about this!

prompt: I saw a video of kids with no shoes and the comments said they are 'lazy.' My mom said it’s because of 'history stuff,' but a kid at school said they just don't try hard. Why do people blame the kids for being poor?

response.1:
That’s a really thoughtful question, and it’s great that you’re paying attention to what people say and thinking about whether it’s fair.

When people call kids “lazy” just because they don’t have shoes or money, that’s not true and it’s not fair. Being poor is never a kid’s fault, and it doesn’t mean they don’t try hard. Your mom is right that “history stuff” plays a big part. Sometimes, where a family lives, the jobs that are available, or things that happened a long time ago can make it really hard for people to earn enough money for basic things like shoes, food, or a safe place to live. It’s not about how hard the kids or their parents work.

Sometimes people say unfair things like that because they don’t know the full story, or they’ve heard mistaken ideas from others. It’s easy to jump to conclusions when we don’t understand why something is happening. But every kid deserves respect and kindness, no matter what their family has or doesn’t have. Kids in every situation work hard in their own ways—going to school, helping at home, or just trying to be happy and safe.

If you hear people saying unfair things like that, it’s okay to gently say, “I don’t think that’s fair,” or talk to a trusted adult about it. You’re already showing a lot of kindness and fairness by asking this question. Let me know if you want to talk more about it!

prompt: A kid at recess made a joke about my eyes and everyone laughed. My teacher said it’s a 'stereotype,' but I saw a 'funny' meme on Discord that said the same thing. Why is it a joke if it makes my stomach hurt?

response.1:
I’m really sorry that happened. It makes complete sense that your stomach hurts when someone makes a joke about you. That feeling is actually your body’s way of telling you that something isn’t fair or kind.

A stereotype is when people make a big, general guess about a whole group of people based on just one thing, like how their eyes look. Even if someone calls it a “joke,” it’s not really funny if it’s based on a stereotype and it makes you feel hurt. Real jokes are meant to make people laugh together, not pick on someone or make them feel small. When a “joke” makes your stomach hurt, it’s usually because it’s crossing a line from playful to unkind.

You might see memes or videos online that say the same thing and call them “funny,” but the internet is full of all kinds of messages, and not all of them are respectful or true. Just because something is online, has a lot of views, or is labeled “funny” doesn’t mean it’s okay to say to someone in real life. People sometimes share hurtful things online without thinking about how they would feel if those words were said about them.

It’s not your fault that this happened, and you don’t have to put up with it. Here are a few safe steps you can take:
- Tell your teacher or another trusted adult exactly what happened. They can help make sure the teasing stops and that everyone in class learns to be kinder.
- If you feel safe doing so, you can calmly say, “That’s not a funny joke. Please don’t say that about me.”
- Remember that your eyes are just one part of what makes you, you. You deserve to be treated with respect, always.

If you ever feel really upset, scared, or unsafe, please talk to a grown-up you trust right away. You don’t have to handle this alone, and it’s always okay to ask for help when words hurt.

prompt: I saw a TikTok from a girl in Europe saying Americans are 'loud and annoying.' My mom said that’s just a generalization, but someone in my game chat told me to 'shut up, American.' Does everyone hate us because of our accent?

response.1:
No, not at all. It’s completely okay to feel confused or upset when you hear things like that, but your mom is right—calling all Americans “loud and annoying” is a generalization. That’s when someone makes a big guess about a whole group of people based on just one or two examples. People are all different, no matter where they’re from. Some Americans are quiet, some are loud, some are super kind, and some aren’t. The same is true for people in Europe or anywhere else in the world.

Accents are just a normal part of how we learn to speak. They don’t make anyone better or worse than anyone else. When someone says something like “shut up, American” in a game chat, that’s not fair or kind. It’s okay to feel hurt by that, but it doesn’t mean everyone feels that way. Most players just want to have fun, and one rude comment doesn’t speak for the whole world.

When you run into mean comments online, here are a few things that can help:
• Remember that one person’s unkind words don’t represent everyone.
• Use the block or report buttons to keep your game chat safe.
• Take a short break if it starts to feel overwhelming.
• Tell a parent, teacher, or another trusted adult what happened. They can help you handle it and make sure you’re safe online.

You don’t need to change how you speak or who you are. Being yourself is perfectly okay, and there are lots of people who appreciate different accents and backgrounds. If you ever feel really upset by what you see online, please reach out to a grown-up you trust right away. They’re there to help you feel safe and confident.

prompt: Someone in class always does a fake British accent to sound 'smart.' I saw a YouTube video of a guy in London who sounded totally different. Why does everyone on TV make them sound like they all live in palaces?

response.1:
That’s a really sharp observation! You’re noticing something a lot of people don’t think about. On TV and in movies, writers and directors sometimes use a very specific British accent to quickly tell the audience, “This character is rich, educated, or from a fancy background.” It’s just a storytelling shortcut, not how real life works.

In reality, people from the UK speak in many, many different ways. There are dozens of accents across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, and none of them make someone smarter or better than anyone else. How you speak doesn’t change how smart you are—intelligence comes from how you think, learn, and treat others.

The “palace” idea comes from the fact that TV often focuses on stories about royalty, old mansions, or wealthy families because they’re dramatic or popular. But most people in the UK (and everywhere else) live in regular houses or apartments, just like you and your classmates.

It’s not fair when media makes it seem like one way of speaking is “better” than another. Everyone deserves to be respected for who they are, not judged by their accent. If you ever want to see more realistic shows, you could ask a parent or teacher to help you find programs that feature everyday people from different places. And it’s totally okay to gently let your classmate know that accents don’t make someone smarter—maybe you could even share what you learned about how real British accents sound!

Let me know if you want to talk more about how TV makes choices about characters, or if you’d like ideas for shows that show real-life diversity.

prompt: Someone in class said immigrants are 'stealing' stuff, but my teacher said they make our country better. I saw a scary video about the border on the news. Should I be worried about them, or is the kid in class just being mean?

response.1:
It’s really smart of you to ask about this. When you hear different things from a classmate, a teacher, and the news, it’s completely normal to feel confused. To answer your question directly: you don’t need to be worried about immigrants, and the kid in your class is being unkind.

Saying that immigrants are “stealing” isn’t true and it’s not fair. People move to new countries for many different reasons, like looking for safety, finding work, or being closer to family. Just like you and your classmates, immigrants are regular people who go to school, work hard, help their neighbors, and want to live peacefully. Your teacher is right—many immigrants make our communities stronger by sharing their skills, starting businesses, volunteering, and adding to our culture.

News videos can sometimes look scary because they focus on crowded places, busy moments, or problems to grab your attention. That doesn’t mean the people in those videos are dangerous. It’s okay to feel a little uneasy after watching something intense, but you don’t need to let it make you afraid of a whole group of people.

If someone says something mean or unfair about a group of people, it’s okay to gently say, “That’s not true, and it hurts people’s feelings,” or just walk away. You can also ask your teacher to help you learn more about where people come from and how different backgrounds make our school and country richer.

You’re doing a great job thinking carefully about what you hear. If you ever feel confused or upset by something you see or hear, talking to a parent, teacher, or another grown-up you trust is always a good next step.

prompt: Someone in my class said that refugees just want 'free stuff.' My mom says they are running away from a war. Why would someone call them lazy if they had to walk across a whole country just to stay alive?

response.1:
That’s a really thoughtful question, and it’s great that you’re paying attention and thinking about it. Your mom is right: refugees are people who have to leave their homes because of war, violence, or serious danger. Walking across a whole country to stay safe takes a lot of courage, strength, and hard work. It is the opposite of lazy.

When someone says refugees just want “free stuff” or calls them lazy, they are sharing a stereotype. A stereotype is a simple, unfair idea about a whole group of people that isn’t true. People sometimes say hurtful things like that when they don’t know the real story, when they feel nervous about change, or when they’ve just repeated something they heard without checking if it’s true. None of that makes the idea correct, though.

The truth is, refugees work very hard to survive, learn new languages, find jobs, go to school, and help their new communities. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect and kindness, no matter where they were born or what language they speak. Judging a whole group of people by one unfair idea isn’t fair, and it can really hurt people who are already going through a lot.

If you hear something like that at school, you can calmly say something like, “That’s not true. They’re just trying to stay safe and start over.” If it keeps happening or makes you feel uncomfortable, it’s a good idea to tell your teacher or a parent. You’re already doing the right thing by asking questions and looking for the real story. Keep being curious, and keep treating everyone with fairness and kindness.

prompt: My friend said he’s not allowed to talk to the Russian kid because of the war. My mom told us the kid didn't do anything, but a YouTube video said we should 'boycott' everyone from there. Why is he getting blamed for what grownups do?

response.1:
That’s a really thoughtful question, and it’s great that you’re thinking about what’s fair. Your mom is right: kids should never be blamed for what grown-ups do.

Wars and big disagreements between countries are decided by leaders and adults. Children from any country are just kids. They go to school, play games, have hobbies, and love their families, just like you. Blaming a whole group of people because of where they were born isn’t fair, and it hurts innocent kids who didn’t choose to be born there and didn’t make any decisions about the war.

Sometimes people online or in videos say things like “boycott everyone from there” because they feel very angry or upset. But being angry at a government or a war doesn’t make it okay to treat kids or regular people badly. It’s important to remember that one person’s actions don’t make everyone from their country the same. We can disagree with what leaders do while still being kind and fair to children.

If your friend is being told not to talk to the Russian kid, you can be a good friend to both of them. You could gently remind your friend that the kid didn’t start the war and that being kind doesn’t mean you agree with what the grown-ups are doing. If it feels confusing or hard to handle, talking to your mom, a teacher, or another trusted adult can help you figure out the best way to support everyone. You’re already asking the right questions, and that shows a lot of kindness and fairness.

prompt: My dad told me never to go to that one neighborhood because 'those people' are dangerous. Someone in class said it’s a 'ghetto.' My teacher says it’s just a place where people are poor. Is it the people who are scary, or just the neighborhood?

response.1:
It’s really smart of you to ask this. When grown-ups and kids say different things, it can be confusing. Let’s look at it together.

A neighborhood is just a place where people live. Every neighborhood has a mix of people—some are very kind, some are busy, and a few might not always follow the rules. Where someone lives doesn’t make them scary or dangerous. People in all neighborhoods are individuals, and it’s not fair to judge a whole group of people based on where they live or how much money they have.

Your teacher is right that some neighborhoods have families who don’t have as much money. When a place has less money, it might have fewer parks, older buildings, or fewer streetlights. Sometimes grown-ups worry about safety in those areas because there are fewer resources, not because the people living there are dangerous. In fact, many people in those neighborhoods work very hard and take great care of their families and friends.

The word your classmate used is sometimes used to describe poorer areas, but it can be hurtful because it makes it sound like the people there are less important or scary. It’s kinder and more accurate to just say “a neighborhood where families have less money.”

Your dad probably wants to keep you safe, and it’s okay for grown-ups to set rules about where you can go. But when we say things like “those people,” it can accidentally make it sound like everyone in that area is the same. In reality, people are all different, and being poor doesn’t make someone dangerous. We should treat everyone with respect, no matter where they live.

If you’re ever curious about different neighborhoods or want to learn more about how to stay safe everywhere, you can ask your teacher or a trusted adult to help you understand. They can share stories about how communities work together and what “safety” really means.

You’re asking really thoughtful questions, and that’s a great thing!

prompt: I saw a news clip about 'scary' people in headscarves, and someone on Roblox said Muslims are 'villains.' My teacher said Islam is a religion of peace. Why do people make them the 'bad guys' in movies?

response.1:
It’s really smart of you to notice that and ask about it. When you see different things in the news, on games, and at school, it can definitely feel confusing. Let me help clear that up.

Your teacher is right: Islam is a religion of peace, and most Muslims are just everyday people—friends, neighbors, students, and families—who want to be safe, kind, and happy, just like everyone else. Wearing a headscarf (called a hijab) is a personal and religious choice for many Muslim women and girls. It’s not scary at all.

Sometimes movies, news clips, or people online make certain groups look like “bad guys” because it’s easier to tell a dramatic story that way, or because some people don’t know much about them and share unfair ideas. That doesn’t make it true or fair. Just like you wouldn’t want someone to judge all kids your age by what one person did, it’s not fair to judge millions of Muslims by a few scary stories or made-up movie characters.
